questions.stem: Which three Republican presidents held office in the United States between 1921 and 1933?
options: Taft, Harding and Hoover
Harding, Coolidge and Hoover
Wilson, Harding and Coolidge
Coolidge, Hoover and Roosevelt
questions.explanation: Warren Harding (1921-1923), Calvin Coolidge (1923-1929) and Herbert Hoover (1929-1933) were all Republicans. Wilson was a Democrat who left office in 1921, and Franklin Roosevelt, a Democrat, took office in March 1933.

questions.stem: Which policy best sums up the approach of Republican governments to the economy in the 1920s?
options: Free trade combined with strict regulation of the banks
Government ownership of the railways and the power companies
Low taxes, high tariffs and light regulation of business
High taxes on the rich to pay for public works schemes
questions.explanation: Republican governments followed a laissez-faire approach: Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon cut income taxes, the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 raised import duties, and business was lightly regulated. Large public works and close bank regulation came later with the New Deal.

questions.stem: The Hawley-Smoot Tariff of 1930 is usually judged to have worsened the Depression because it:
options: lowered duties so that cheap imports drove US factories out of business
forced American farmers to sell their crops overseas at a fixed price
ended the war debt payments that European nations owed to the US
led other countries to raise their own tariffs, shrinking world trade
questions.explanation: Hawley-Smoot raised US duties on thousands of imports, and many trading partners retaliated with tariffs of their own. World trade fell sharply, hurting American exporters, especially farmers. It raised rather than lowered duties.

questions.stem: American farmers struggled through most of the 1920s mainly because:
options: the government fixed food prices below production costs
overproduction after the war pushed crop prices down
a shortage of tractors meant they could not plant crops
Prohibition closed the main market for their wheat
questions.explanation: Farmers had expanded output during the First World War, and when European demand fell after 1918, surpluses drove prices down. Many farmers were left in debt for land and machinery bought during the boom years.

questions.stem: 'Buying on the margin' contributed to the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 because investors:
options: had to pay the whole price of each share in gold before trading began
bought shares with borrowed money and were forced to sell when prices fell
were forbidden by law from selling any shares until they had held them a full year
could buy shares only from the federal government at fixed prices
questions.explanation: Margin buying let investors pay a small deposit and borrow the rest from brokers. When prices fell, brokers demanded repayment, forcing sales that drove prices down further. There was no rule requiring payment in gold or a one-year holding period.

questions.stem: Which combination of long-term weaknesses do historians most often link to the onset of the Great Depression?
options: Unequal income, overproduction, weak banks and reliance on credit
High wages, labour shortages, strong unions and rising farm prices
Heavy federal spending, high income taxes and a large budget deficit
Free trade, falling factory output and a shrinking money supply in 1925
questions.explanation: Historians point to unequal income that limited demand, overproduction in farming and industry, thousands of small unregulated banks and heavy use of credit. Wages had not kept pace with output, unions were weak, and federal spending and taxes were low.

questions.stem: Thousands of small US banks failed between 1930 and 1933. Why was each failure so damaging?
options: The Federal Reserve was required by law to close every rural bank
Banks held only government bonds, and these became worthless after 1929
Each failed bank had to repay its debts to European governments
Deposits were not insured, so savers lost their money and spending fell
questions.explanation: Before 1933 there was no federal deposit insurance, so a bank failure wiped out savers and frightened others into withdrawing money, spreading panic. Roosevelt's Banking Act of 1933 created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to stop this.

questions.stem: Shanty towns of the homeless that grew up on the edges of US cities in the early 1930s were known as:
options: Hoovervilles
Coolidge camps
Dust Bowls
Okie towns
questions.explanation: The camps were mockingly named after President Hoover, who was blamed for not doing enough. 'Okies' was the name for displaced farmers from Oklahoma and nearby states, and the Dust Bowl was the drought-stricken region of the southern Plains.

questions.stem: How did the Dust Bowl of the 1930s affect farming families on the southern Great Plains?
options: Floods destroyed the cotton crop, and families moved to northern cities
Locust plagues ate the wheat, and the government bought all their land
Early frosts killed the fruit, and farmers joined the Civilian Conservation Corps
Drought and dust storms ruined farms, and many migrated west to California
questions.explanation: Years of drought combined with over-ploughing turned topsoil to dust, which storms blew away. Many families, often called Okies, headed to California seeking farm work, a migration shown in Steinbeck's novel The Grapes of Wrath.

questions.stem: Unemployment in the United States reached its peak in 1933 at about:
options: one in twenty workers
one in two workers
one in four workers
one in ten workers
questions.explanation: Official estimates put unemployment at about 25 per cent in 1933, more than 12 million people. It fell under the New Deal but remained high for the rest of the decade.

questions.stem: African Americans were often described as 'last hired, first fired' during the Depression. This meant that they:
options: were hired first by New Deal agencies and dismissed when work ended
were the only workers allowed to join the new industrial unions
lost jobs before white workers and found it harder to be rehired
were protected by law from losing work during the economic downturn
questions.explanation: Discrimination meant African American workers were laid off first and taken back last, so their unemployment rate was well above that of white workers. New Deal programs also often paid them less or excluded them.

questions.stem: Which statement about women's experience of the Great Depression is most accurate?
options: Women were unaffected because almost none of them had worked for wages before 1929
Many married women lost jobs to men, yet the share of women in paid work rose slightly
Women were banned by federal law from all paid work until the New Deal began in 1933
Women's unemployment was far higher than men's because factories employed only women
questions.explanation: Many employers and some governments dismissed married women to give jobs to men, but women were concentrated in clerical and service work that was hit less hard than heavy industry, so their share of the workforce grew a little. No federal law banned women from work.

questions.stem: Herbert Hoover's response to the Depression is best described as:
options: voluntary action by business and local relief, with limited federal aid
nationalising the banks and the railways to keep Americans in work
refusing to take any federal action at all during his presidency
creating Social Security and unemployment insurance as early as 1930
questions.explanation: Hoover believed in 'rugged individualism' and asked business leaders to keep wages up voluntarily, leaving relief to charities and local government. He did take some federal action, such as the Reconstruction Finance Corporation of 1932, so 'no action at all' is wrong. Social Security came in 1935 under Roosevelt.

questions.stem: The Reconstruction Finance Corporation, set up under Hoover in 1932, was designed to:
options: lend money to banks, railways and large businesses
give direct cash payments to unemployed families
employ young men in forestry and conservation work
buy surplus crops from farmers at guaranteed prices
questions.explanation: The RFC made loans to banks, railways and big companies, hoping the benefits would reach ordinary people. Critics said it helped business rather than the hungry. Forestry work for young men was Roosevelt's Civilian Conservation Corps.

questions.stem: In July 1932 the army drove the Bonus Army out of Washington. Why did this event damage Hoover's standing?
options: It revealed that Hoover had secretly cut all veterans' pensions in half
It caused a run on the banks that closed every bank in the capital
It led Congress to remove Hoover from office before the election
It showed troops being used against unemployed veterans asking for help
questions.explanation: Thousands of First World War veterans camped in Washington to demand early payment of a promised bonus. Images of soldiers clearing them with tear gas and burning their camp made Hoover seem uncaring, a few months before he lost the 1932 election to Roosevelt.

questions.stem: What were Franklin Roosevelt's 'fireside chats'?
options: Newspaper columns he wrote each week throughout his presidency
Debates in Congress over the passing of New Deal laws
Radio broadcasts explaining his policies directly to Americans
Private meetings with business leaders at the White House
questions.explanation: Beginning in March 1933 with a talk on the banking crisis, Roosevelt used radio to speak to Americans in a calm, personal way. The broadcasts helped restore confidence in the banks and in government.

questions.stem: During the 'Hundred Days' after his inauguration in March 1933, Roosevelt first acted to:
options: raise taxes on all workers to balance the federal budget
repeal Prohibition by presidential order without Congress
nationalise the steel and coal industries under federal control
close the banks briefly and reopen only those judged sound
questions.explanation: Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday and Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act, which allowed sound banks to reopen under federal supervision. Confidence returned and deposits flowed back. Prohibition was ended by the Twenty-first Amendment, ratified in December 1933, not by presidential order.

questions.stem: Which New Deal agency built dams to provide flood control and electricity across a poor region of the South?
options: National Recovery Administration
Tennessee Valley Authority
Civilian Conservation Corps
Works Progress Administration
questions.explanation: The Tennessee Valley Authority, created in 1933, built dams that controlled flooding, generated cheap power and helped develop a poor region. The CCC employed young men in conservation, and the NRA set industry codes.

questions.stem: The Social Security Act of 1935 is significant because it:
options: created old-age pensions and unemployment insurance funded by payroll taxes
guaranteed every adult American a government job at a minimum wage
gave all workers the legal right to join unions and to bargain collectively
paid farmers to reduce the amount of land they planted each year
questions.explanation: The Act set up a federal system of old-age pensions and unemployment insurance, a lasting change in the role of government. The right to bargain collectively came from the Wagner Act of 1935, and paying farmers to cut output was the Agricultural Adjustment Act.

questions.stem: In Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935), the Supreme Court:
options: upheld Roosevelt's plan to add six new judges to the court
ruled that the Social Security Act breached states' rights
ordered the government to close down the Tennessee Valley Authority
struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act as unconstitutional
questions.explanation: The court ruled unanimously that the NIRA gave too much power to the president and regulated trade within states. Roosevelt's 1937 plan to add judges, the 'court-packing' plan, was defeated in Congress, and the Social Security Act was upheld in 1937.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that the New Deal did not end the Great Depression?
options: The Tennessee Valley Authority brought electricity to farms in seven southern states
Roosevelt was re-elected in 1936 in one of the largest landslides in US history
The Wagner Act led to rapid growth in union membership during the later 1930s
Unemployment rose again in the recession of 1937-38 and stayed high until rearmament
questions.explanation: When Roosevelt cut spending in 1937, the economy slipped back into recession and unemployment rose, and full employment returned only with wartime production. The other evidence shows New Deal achievements or popularity, not a failure to end the Depression.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the New Deal's greatest success was political rather than economic. Which evidence best supports this?
options: It cut unemployment to under 2 per cent before the end of Roosevelt's first term
It balanced the federal budget every year between 1933 and 1939
It ended racial discrimination in federal relief and job programs
It restored faith in democratic government when dictators were rising elsewhere
questions.explanation: Many historians argue that the New Deal's greatest achievement was keeping Americans' faith in democracy and capitalism at a time of fascism and communism abroad. Unemployment stayed well above 10 per cent, budgets were in deficit, and relief programs often discriminated.

questions.stem: The 1920 US census showed for the first time that:
options: most Americans had been born outside the United States
more Americans lived in urban areas than in rural areas
more Americans worked in farming than in all other jobs
the population had fallen since the previous census
questions.explanation: The 1920 census recorded just over half the population living in urban areas, as people moved to cities for factory and office jobs. The population was growing, and farming was a shrinking share of employment.

questions.stem: Which development most helped Americans buy cars, radios and refrigerators in the 1920s?
options: Laws fixing the price of electrical appliances
Hire purchase, or buying on instalment credit
Government subsidies paid to every consumer
A rise in tariffs on European manufactured goods
questions.explanation: Instalment buying let families pay a small amount up front and the rest over time, which greatly expanded the market for consumer goods. Advertising also encouraged spending. There were no consumer subsidies or price-fixing laws.

questions.stem: How did the mass-produced motor car change American society in the 1920s?
options: It ended the movement of people from rural areas to the large cities
It was limited to the rich because each car was built entirely by hand
It encouraged suburbs, roads and new industries such as oil and rubber
It reduced the demand for steel because cars were mostly made of wood
questions.explanation: Cheap cars like the Model T led to road building, the growth of suburbs and booms in steel, oil, glass and rubber. They gave families new freedom of movement. Assembly-line production made cars affordable to many, not just the rich.

questions.stem: The Jazz Singer (1927) is significant in the history of American entertainment as:
options: the first film to be shown in colour in American cinemas
the first jazz recording sold on a gramophone record
the first feature-length film with synchronised talking scenes
the first radio program broadcast to every state simultaneously
questions.explanation: The Jazz Singer, starring Al Jolson, included synchronised speech and songs and launched the era of 'talkies'. Hollywood became a huge industry, and cinema attendance remained high even during the Depression.

questions.stem: The Immigration Act of 1924 limited immigration by:
options: setting national quotas that favoured northern and western Europeans
banning all immigrants from Europe for a period of ten years
allowing entry only to those immigrants who could speak English fluently
giving priority to immigrants from Japan and other parts of Asia
questions.explanation: The Act set quotas of 2 per cent of each nationality living in the US in 1890, which favoured northern and western Europeans and cut arrivals from southern and eastern Europe. It also barred immigration from Japan, which caused resentment there.

questions.stem: The Scopes 'Monkey' Trial of 1925 in Tennessee is best seen as evidence of:
options: growing support for Prohibition in the cities of the North
the federal government's efforts to control state school systems
conflict between religious fundamentalism and modern scientific ideas
conflict between the trade unions and employers over teachers' wages
questions.explanation: John Scopes was tried for teaching evolution in breach of a state law. The case set rural fundamentalists against urban modernists and is a key example of the urban-rural divide of the 1920s. Scopes was convicted, though the verdict was later overturned on a technicality.

questions.stem: Why did Prohibition lead to a growth in organised crime?
options: Police were banned from arresting anyone connected with the sale of alcohol
Prohibition made gambling legal, which attracted criminal gangs to cities
Unemployed brewery workers were forced into crime by the closure of the bars
Gangsters made huge profits supplying illegal alcohol to willing customers
questions.explanation: Demand for alcohol continued, and gangs such as Al Capone's in Chicago made fortunes from bootlegging and speakeasies, using bribery and violence. Capone was finally convicted of tax evasion in 1931. Prohibition was repealed in 1933.

questions.stem: The Red Scare of 1919-1920, including the Palmer Raids, was mainly a reaction to:
options: anger over the Senate's rejection of the League of Nations
anger over the stock market crash and bank failures
fear of communist revolution, strikes and anarchist bombings
fear of Japanese expansion in the Pacific and in China
questions.explanation: After the Russian Revolution, a wave of strikes and a series of bombings by anarchists in 1919 made many Americans fear revolution. Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer's raids arrested thousands of suspected radicals, many of them immigrants, and hundreds were deported.

questions.stem: The Sacco and Vanzetti case (1921-1927) is often used to illustrate social tension in the 1920s because:
options: two union leaders were jailed for organising the Boston police strike of 1919
two bootleggers who were acquitted after bribing the jury in a Chicago murder trial
two Italian anarchist immigrants were executed after a trial many saw as prejudiced
two African American workers were lynched after a strike in the steel industry
questions.explanation: Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti were convicted of a robbery and murder and executed in 1927. Many people believed their Italian origin and anarchist beliefs weighed more than the evidence, linking the case to nativism and the Red Scare.

questions.stem: Which development shows racial conflict in the United States in the years after the First World War?
options: The Supreme Court ended segregation in all southern schools
The Great Migration of African Americans moved south
The Ku Klux Klan grew to millions of members by the mid-1920s
Congress passed a federal law banning lynching in 1922
questions.explanation: The revived Klan targeted African Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants and had millions of members at its peak in the mid-1920s. Anti-lynching bills failed in the Senate, school segregation was not ruled unconstitutional until 1954, and the Great Migration went north.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why trade union membership fell during the 1920s?
options: Employers used open-shop drives and company unions, and courts issued injunctions against strikes
The federal government passed laws that made membership of any union a criminal offence
Most workers moved to farms, where unions were not permitted to organise members
Unions disbanded voluntarily because wages had risen faster than prices in every industry
questions.explanation: After defeats in the 1919 strikes, employers promoted the 'open shop', company unions and welfare schemes, and courts readily issued injunctions against strikes. Union membership was not illegal, and the Wagner Act of 1935 later reversed the trend.

questions.stem: Why did the United States never join the League of Nations?
options: The US was still at war with Germany in 1920
The Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles
The League's members voted to exclude the US
President Wilson opposed the creation of the League
questions.explanation: Although President Wilson had proposed the League, the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, which included the League Covenant. Opponents such as Henry Cabot Lodge feared it would drag the US into foreign wars.

questions.stem: Which action shows that the US was not completely isolationist in the 1920s?
options: It signed a military alliance with Britain and France in 1925
It sent troops to occupy the Rhineland after the French did
It hosted the Washington Naval Conference of 1921-22 to limit warships
It joined the League of Nations as a non-voting member state in 1926
questions.explanation: The Washington Conference produced treaties limiting battleships for the US, Britain, Japan, France and Italy. The US also arranged the Dawes Plan (1924) and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928), but it never joined the League or formed military alliances.

questions.stem: The Dawes Plan of 1924 was designed to:
options: set a limit on the size of the navies of the major powers
outlaw war as a way of settling disputes between nations
reschedule German reparations and provide American loans to Germany
cancel all of the war debts that Britain and France owed to the US
questions.explanation: Charles Dawes's plan reduced Germany's annual reparation payments and arranged loans, mainly from American banks, so Germany could pay Britain and France, who could then repay war debts to the US. Outlawing war was the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928.

questions.stem: The Neutrality Acts passed by Congress between 1935 and 1937 were mainly a response to:
options: Roosevelt's wish to sell weapons to the Allies
public fear of being drawn into another European war
Japanese attacks on American merchant ships in the Pacific
pressure from Britain for an American alliance
questions.explanation: Isolationist feeling was strong, fed by the Nye Committee's claim that bankers and arms makers had drawn the US into the First World War. The Acts banned arms sales and loans to nations at war. Roosevelt later sought to loosen them to help Britain and France.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the US moving step by step towards support for Britain before Pearl Harbor?
options: Lend-Lease (1939), cash and carry (1940), destroyers-for-bases (1941)
Destroyers-for-bases (1939), Lend-Lease (1940), cash and carry (1941)
Cash and carry (1939), Lend-Lease (1940), destroyers-for-bases (1941)
Cash and carry (1939), destroyers-for-bases (1940), Lend-Lease (1941)
questions.explanation: In November 1939 Congress allowed warring nations to buy arms for cash and carry them away. In September 1940 the US gave Britain 50 old destroyers in exchange for bases, and in March 1941 Lend-Lease allowed aid without payment. Each step reflected Roosevelt working within domestic opposition to war.

questions.stem: In mid-1941 the US froze Japanese assets and cut off oil exports to Japan. Why did this make war more likely?
options: Japan relied on imported oil and saw seizing Southeast Asian resources as its alternative
Japan had publicly promised to attack the US if any trade restrictions were imposed on it
The embargo also stopped American food exports, causing famine across Japan
The embargo broke a treaty of alliance that the US and Japan had signed in 1937
questions.explanation: Japan imported most of its oil, much of it from the US. After Japanese troops moved into southern Indochina, the embargo forced Japan to choose between withdrawing from China or seizing the oil of the Dutch East Indies, which meant war with the US. Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941.

questions.stem: Which factor best shows how domestic pressures shaped US foreign policy in the late 1930s?
options: Congress voted to join the League of Nations after the fall of France in 1940
Strong isolationist opinion, including the America First Committee, limited Roosevelt's options
Business leaders demanded war with Germany to end the Depression and gain new markets
African American voters forced Roosevelt into declaring war on Italy once it invaded Ethiopia
questions.explanation: Public opinion and Congress were strongly against involvement in war, and groups such as the America First Committee campaigned against aid to Britain. Roosevelt therefore moved cautiously, presenting aid as a way to keep America out of war. The US never joined the League.
